Council of Ferrara-Florence
ko͞un´sĭl ŏv fĕ-rä´ra flŏr´ens
n. (the Council of Ferrara-Florence, 1438–1445, the attempted reunion of the Greek and Latin churches, signed by the Greeks under political duress and repudiated at Constantinople)
Latin concilium; opened at Ferrara in 1438 and moved to Florence in 1439 because of plague and the cost.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Council of Ferrara-Florence was convened as the Ottoman armies closed on Constantinople. The Emperor John VIII came west in person with the patriarch and a large delegation, because reunion with Rome was the price of a crusade to save the city. For months the Greeks argued the filioque, purgatory, unleavened bread and the papal primacy; worn down, short of money, far from home and under the plainest political necessity, all but one signed the decree Laetentur Caeli in July 1439. The one was Mark of Ephesus, who refused and whom the East has honoured ever since. The union collapsed on contact with reality: the clergy and people of Constantinople rejected it, the promised help never came in force, and the city fell in 1453. It is the classic case of agreement purchased rather than reached. 2Co 6:14 governs the terms on which the church may unite, Amo 3:3 asks “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?”, and Jer 8:11 names the result: “they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines union as the act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a single body; and concord as agreement between persons.

expand to see more

UN'ION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body or a mixture.

2. Concord; agreement and conjunction of mind, will, affections or interest.

CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.

Key Scripture

2Co 6:14 — "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?"

Amo 3:3 — "Can two walk together, except they be agreed?"

Gal 2:5 — "To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you."

Jer 8:11 — "For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace."

Modern Corruption

Florence is the proof that a union signed under necessity is not a union, and that the churches which trade doctrine for help get neither.

expand to see more

The Greeks did not change their minds at Florence; they changed their signatures. Reunion was the condition of military aid, and a confession produced by that pressure bound nobody, which the reception at home immediately showed. The permanent lesson is about the nature of agreement: it is the mind persuaded from Scripture, or it is nothing. Gal 2:5 shows the apostle refusing to give place “by subjection, no, not for an hour” where the truth of the gospel was at stake, and he was under pressure too. Every ecumenical instrument since has had to reckon with Florence, which is why honest dialogue begins by asking what has actually been believed, not what can be signed.

The second corruption is the modern treatment of Mark of Ephesus's refusal as mere obstinacy, the one man who would not be reasonable while a city burned. He has the better of it. If the filioque and the papal primacy are what each side said they were, then no emergency makes them negotiable, and a man who signs what he does not believe has lied in the name of peace. The Reformed answer is not Rome's and not the East's, but the method is Mark's: hold what Scripture proves, decline what it does not, and refuse to buy concord with a false subscription.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek heterozugeo (G2086), to be unequally yoked; koinonia (G2842), fellowship; Hebrew yaad (H3259), to be agreed, to appoint a meeting.

Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be yoked with another kind; 2 Corinthians 6:14.

Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, partnership; 2 Corinthians 6:14.

Hebrew yaad (H3259) — to appoint, to be agreed; Amos 3:3.

Greek hupotage (G5292) — subjection; Galatians 2:5.

Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be slight, to make light of; Jeremiah 8:11.

Usage

"“Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14) — the terms of lawful union."

"“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — the question Florence evaded."

"“Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 8:11) — the decree of 1439."
